hints: Count the total electrons present in each species first. Carbon is atomic number 6, so work out how many electrons are in C, in C+ and in C-.
Remember how electrons fill degenerate p orbitals. Paired electrons go in 1s and 2s first, then 2p electrons stay unpaired in separate orbitals where possible.
walkthrough:
Count electrons for atom and ions**
Think of this as simple bookkeeping. A carbon atom has $6$ electrons. Removing one electron to make $\text{C}^{+}$ leaves $5$ electrons. Adding one electron to make $\text{C}^{-}$ gives $7$ electrons. The 1s level is already drawn filled, so you only need to place the rest.

Fill 2s then 2p in energy order**
The 2s orbital comes next above 1s and always fills as a pair: $\uparrow\downarrow$. That uses 2 electrons in every case. So carbon atom has $2$ electrons left for 2p, $\text{C}^{+}$ has $1$ left, $\text{C}^{-}$ has $3$ left. Draw 2p as three equal energy boxes above 2s.

Apply Hund's rule to the 2p electrons**
When orbitals have exactly the same energy, electrons prefer to sit alone first. So for the carbon atom put one up arrow in two different 2p boxes. For $\text{C}^{+}$ put one up arrow in one box. For $\text{C}^{-}$ put one up arrow in each of the three boxes. No pairing in 2p here.

Final answer: All three species: 1s $\uparrow\downarrow$, 2s $\uparrow\downarrow$ with 2s above 1s and 2p above 2s.
Carbon atom ($6e^{-}$): 2p $\uparrow$ $\uparrow$ ; $\text{C}^{+}$ ion ($5e^{-}$): 2p $\uparrow$ ; $\text{C}^{-}$ ion ($7e^{-}$): 2p $\uparrow$ $\uparrow$ $\uparrow$.

hints: Look at each carbon in the cage. Each carbon is joined to three other carbons with one double bond character, very like graphite or an alkene carbon.
walkthrough:
See the bonding pattern around each carbon**
Zoom in on any black dot in the diagram. It connects to three neighbours in a curved network of alternating single and double bonds. That means three sigma bonds plus one p orbital used for pi bonding, exactly the same as in graphite and in $\text{C}=\text{C}$. That arrangement is $\text{sp}^{2}$ hybridisation.

hints: If each carbon is sp2 in C60, think what must happen when hydrogen adds. Each C=C double bond can take one H2, converting sp2 carbons to sp3 with one H per carbon.
walkthrough:
Link hybridisation to hydrogen uptake**
$\text{sp}^{2}$ tells you every carbon is part of an unsaturated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ system. Hydrogenation adds across each double bond, breaking the pi bond and giving each carbon one extra sigma bond to H. With excess hydrogen, every carbon becomes $\text{sp}^{3}$.

Count H atoms needed**
There are $60$ carbons, each can accept one H atom when fully saturated. So $60$ H atoms add in total, giving $\text{C}_{60}\text{H}_{60}$. That is why $x = 60$.

hints: Compare where chlorine has gone. In reaction 1 it is on the side chain to give $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$, in reaction 2 it is on the ring ortho to the methyl group.
Recall the two classic ways methylbenzene reacts with chlorine. One needs light to attack the alkane-like side chain, the other needs a halogen carrier catalyst to attack the benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Recognise side chain versus ring attack**
Look closely at the products. Reaction 1 keeps the benzene ring untouched and puts Cl on the $\text{CH}_{3}$ group to make $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$. That is substitution of an alkane type C-H bond. Reaction 2 keeps the $\text{CH}_{3}$ intact and puts Cl directly on the ring, ortho to $\text{CH}_{3}$. That is electrophilic substitution on the aromatic ring.

Choose conditions to direct the chlorine**
For the side chain, you need chlorine radicals, so use $\text{Cl}_{2}$ with UV light: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}_{2} \xrightarrow{UV} \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$ For the ring, you need a strong electrophile $\text{Cl}^{+}$, so use $\text{Cl}_{2}$ with $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ carrier in the dark at room temperature: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{AlCl}_{3}} \text{ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{HCl}$$

Final answer: reaction 1: $\text{Cl}_{2}$ with UV light (or sunlight, high temperature)
reaction 2: $\text{Cl}_{2}$ with $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ (or $\text{FeCl}_{3}$, $\text{Fe}$) catalyst, no UV light

hints: Think about what UV light does to a Cl-Cl bond and what type of reactive species then attacks the methyl side chain.
walkthrough:
Connect light to radicals**
UV light splits $\text{Cl}_{2}$ by homolytic fission into two $\text{Cl} \cdot$ radicals. Those radicals then substitute H atoms on the $\text{CH}_{3}$ side chain in a chain reaction. Any reaction that substitutes via radicals in this way is called free radical substitution.

hints: With excess chlorine under the same side chain conditions, substitution does not stop after one H. Think what happens to all three H atoms of the CH3 group.
walkthrough:
Push side chain substitution to completion**
Picture the $\text{CH}_{3}$ group. One $\text{H}$ is replaced to give $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$, but with plenty of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ the remaining C-H bonds are also attacked by $\text{Cl} \cdot$ radicals. All three H atoms are eventually replaced, leaving $\text{CCl}_{3}$ attached to the unchanged benzene ring: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{3} + 3\text{Cl}_{2} \xrightarrow{UV} \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CCl}_{3} + 3\text{HCl}$$ So draw a benzene ring bonded to $\text{CCl}_{3}$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CCl}_{3}$, benzene ring with a $\text{CCl}_{3}$ substituent
